info.bio:
The Kingsmen es una banda norteamericana de garage rock de los años 1960. Se formaron en Portland, Oregon. Son conocidos por su versión de la canción de Richard Berry "Louie Louie". Este sencillo los ubicó en el nº 2 en el Billboard durante seis semanas. Esta versión de "Louie Louie" es considerada como todo un clásico.

Louie Louie

Cuando se grabó este sencillo la banda era conformada por Jack Ely (cantante/guitarra rítmica), Lynn Easton (batería), Mike Mitchell (guitarra), Don Gallucci (piano) y Bob Nordby (bajo).

scenes.name: Warhol, la Factory y el pop de 1966
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En la primavera de 1966 Warhol era el artista más famoso de Estados Unidos y ya no hacía arte en el sentido tradicional: había anunciado en 1965 que dejaba la pintura por el cine, la gente y los entornos totales. La Factory de la calle 47 Este era a la vez cadena de producción de serigrafías, plató y escenario abierto; un espejo de la sociedad neoyorquina donde lo que esta despreciaba (drag queens, yonquis, chaperos, perturbados) podía volverse superstar. Sus cuadros devolvían a América sus valores (sexo, muerte, crimen, fama, dinero, producción en masa) y sus series de desastres el regodeo mediático en la muerte. Obrero gay de Pittsburgh con una rabia de outsider, se convirtió en estrella de rock en el caos de su retrospectiva de Filadelfia (octubre de 1965). Gloria Steinem lo puso en el centro de la cultura pop en Life y Susan Sontag hizo de lo camp una obsesión; Batman, A Clockwork Orange, el caso de los asesinatos de Tucson y Capote alimentaban el aire de violencia que él recortaba de las revistas. Con la anfetamina el ambiente se volvió paranoico y cruel; Danny Williams, su amante y autor de las luces del EPI, desapareció en julio. Durante 1966, sin pretenderlo, «se convirtió en América».

scenes.name: Los rockers de garaje
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En 1966 no tenían nombre (Billboard los llamaba «rockers»); hoy se les llama grupos de garaje. La respuesta creativa americana a la invasión británica: chicos blancos de suburbio que ensayaban en el garaje familiar y tocaban en gimnasios, iglesias y fiestas, con cortes de pelo de Brian Jones, actitud de Jagger, fuzz, rave-ups a lo Yardbirds, Them y Stones y, casi siempre, un órgano Farfisa o Vox con un regusto siniestro de película de terror de autocine. Recuperaban la línea del rock americano de 1963-1964 (Kingsmen, Trashmen) que los Beatles cortaron en seco: «Hanky Panky» de Tommy James, grabado en 1963, fue número 1 en julio de 1966. Ese septiembre las listas se llenaron de discos duros: «96 Tears» de ? and the Mysterians (mexicanoamericanos de Flint, con un órgano hipnótico de otro disco), «Dirty Water» de los Standells, «You’re Gonna Miss Me» de los 13th Floor Elevators y «Psychotic Reaction» de Count Five, calco del «I’m a Man» de los Yardbirds. Quejas dirigidas a las mujeres, pero también una nueva confianza; quejas pequeñas que empezaban a encontrar un objetivo, como en «One of These Days» de los Roosters.

scenes.name: El diluvio: invasión británica y garage
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El Mersey-beat lleva a su conclusión la idea de los Beach Boys (ritmo de rock'n'roll y melodía pop): los Beatles, «la segunda gran estafa del rock'n'roll», popularizan lo que surge del underground. Frente a ellos, las tres grandes bandas británicas de 1964: los Rolling Stones (que redefinen al intérprete, el concierto y la canción rock y fijan el eje cantante-chamán y guitarrista carismático), los Kinks (inventores del riff más famoso y del garage, el hard rock y el heavy metal) y los Animals; los Who llevan al límite el himno generacional y la ópera rock, y los Yardbirds establecen la supremacía de la guitarra. En EE UU la invasión británica desata el garage-rock, los proto-punks de cada ciudad (Kingsmen, Sonics, Standells, ? and the Mysterians, Monks).

podcast.title: Lynn Easton's Departure and Death (1968-2023)
podcast.body: Lynn Easton left music in 1968, giving the Kingsmen's name to Mike Mitchell, the lead guitarist and only other remaining original member. Easton passed away in April 2023, with the cause of death unknown due to his religious beliefs precluding medical consultation. "Linne Eastern quit music in 1968, giving the King's men's name to the league guitarist Mike Mitchell, the only other original member still in the band. Eastern died in April this year. No one sure what off as his religious beliefs meant he never saw a doctor."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Jack Ely's Solo Touring and Death (until 2015)
podcast.body: Jack Ely continued to tour solo, performing his one hit, "Louie Louie," until his death in 2015. "Jackie Lee toured solo playing his one hit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Boston DJ's "Worst Record of the Week" Sparked Demand (October)
podcast.body: In October, Boston DJ Arnie "Woo Woo" Ginzburg, who despised The Kingsmen's "Louie Louie," played it twice during his "worst record of the week" segment. This unexpected negative exposure generated immense public interest, resulting in 50 calls from record shops the next day as customers sought the record. "This one was a DJ in Boston, and the most popular DJ in the area, and he hated the record. He hated it so much he played it on his show, because he had a slot called the worst record of the week."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Christian Scientist Background
podcast.body: Jack Ely and Lynn Easton, the core members of The Kingsmen, were lifelong friends from Christian Scientist families actively involved in their local church. "Both families were Christian scientists and actively involved in their local church, and they had grown up together."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Easton Family Support and Management
podcast.body: Lynn Easton's parents supported the band; his father became their manager, and his mother registered the group's name at the local courthouse. "But Easton's did, and Easton's father became the group's manager. Easton's mother even went to the local courthouse to register the group's name for them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Ely's Stepfather's Disapproval of Music
podcast.body: Although Jack Ely's biological father was a professional singer, his stepfather, after his mother remarried, discouraged Ely from pursuing music. "Ely's biological father had been a professional singer, but when the father died and Ely's mother remarried, his stepfather didn't want him to have anything to do with music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: FBI Obscenity Investigation (2.5 Years)
podcast.body: The Kingsmen's "Louie Louie" became the subject of a two-and-a-half-year FBI investigation for obscenity due to Jack Ely's slurred vocals, which led people to imagine dirty lyrics. Despite extensive analysis at various speeds, interviews, and obtaining the mono master tape, the FBI found no audible obscenities, inadvertently missing Lynn Easton's actual yelled expletive. "And obviously the FBI spent two years investigating the song. On the FBI website you can read 119 pages of memos from FBI agents"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: House Band at Producer's Club
podcast.body: The Kingsmen were the house band at an all-ages club owned by the local DJ from Portland radio station 91 Kissin, who also produced their famous recording of "Louis Louis." "He owned an all-ages club that featured the Kingsman, which is the band we're talking about here, as the house band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Initial Poor Sales (Hundreds of Copies)
podcast.body: Upon its initial release, The Kingsmen's "Louie Louie" sold only a couple of hundred copies, significantly less than The Raiders' version, and was rejected by Capitol Records as "the worst garbage." "while the Raiders were selling thousands, the Kingsmen only sold a couple of hundred copies."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Launch of American Garage Band Era
podcast.body: The Kingsmen are credited with launching the era of the American garage band. These groups were typically rough, ragged, and occasionally incorporated risqué material into their music. "The Kingsman launched the era of the American garage band, groups that were often rough and ragged, and who got risque from time to time within material."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lynn Easton's Attempted Coup (August)
podcast.body: In August, Lynn Easton attempted to seize control of the band, announcing he would become the lead singer and Jack Ely the drummer. He leveraged the fact that his mother had registered the band name solely in his name, leading Ely and other members to quit. "In August, Eastern decided that he was going to stop being the drummer and be the lead singer instead. He told Ealy that Ealy was going to be the drummer now."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Managerial Change to Ken Chase
podcast.body: Lynn Easton's father was replaced as manager by Ken Chase, the owner of the radio station where Roger Hart was the most popular DJ. "Easton's father was replaced as their manager by Ken Chase, the owner of the radio station where Roger Hart was the most popular DJ"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mike Mitchell's Continuation of The Kingsmen
podcast.body: Mike Mitchell's lineup of The Kingsmen continued to perform until the Covid-19 pandemic and is expected to resume touring once the pandemic subsides. "Mitchell's lineup of King's men continued to perform until Covid happened, and will presumably do so again once the pandemic is over."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: National Distribution and Chart Ascent
podcast.body: Prompted by reports of high sales in Boston, Malf Schlacht of Scepter Records picked up The Kingsmen's "Louie Louie" for national distribution through their Wand subsidiary. It sold 21,000 copies in Boston in its first week and rapidly climbed the charts, reaching number 2 by December 14, 1963. "Malf Schlacht of its septer heard from the distributors how well the record was doing, and picked it up for national distribution on their one subsidiary."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Portland's Second Best Band
podcast.body: The Kingsmen were a group of teenagers who, even on a good day, were considered at best the second-best band in Portland, significantly outmatched by Paul Revere and The Raiders. "There were a bunch of teenagers who had formed a group a few years earlier, and even on a good day they were at best the second best band in Portland, with the Raiders far far ahead."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Singer's Enunciation Issues
podcast.body: The lead singer of The Kingsmen, Jack Ely, wore heavy braces on his teeth and was forced to sing upwards into a single overhead microphone, which contributed to his inability to enunciate the lyrics clearly. "The singer wore these heavy braces on his teeth, and he was forced to sing up into a single overhead microphone so don't wonder he couldn't enunciate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unintelligible Lyrics Controversy
podcast.body: The unclear lyrics of The Kingsmen's "Louie Louie" led to significant controversy. Some politicians believed the song contained very dirty and dangerous messages, leading the governor of Indiana to ban it. The FBI even launched an 18-month investigation, shadowing the group on tour, but ultimately concluded that the lyrics were "unintelligible at any speed." "Some politicians believed he was singing something very, very dirty and therefore dangerous."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Unprofessional Recording Session
podcast.body: The Kingsmen's recording session for "Louie Louie" was marked by unprofessionalism; the members had to collectively pay the $50 fee themselves when their manager disclaimed responsibility, in stark contrast to The Raiders' funded session in the same studio that week. "the members of the group had to dig through their pockets and get together in the $50 themselves."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Late 80s/Early 90s Garage Punk Band
xref.body: The Headcoats are cited as an example of a Garage Punk band from the minor revival in the late 1980s and early 1990s. These bands typically played louder and faster, taking more influence from The Stooges than The Kingsmen. "You might have heard of bands like the headcoats and the mighty seasors and the mummies, or maybe not."
